reasons: Lake identity gives case_name United States v. Porter, court 5th Cir., docket 25-60163, date_decided 2026-03-17, year 2026.

residual_risks: Only the official-citation flag is defective; the case identity and slip citation survive.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Display or metadata should explicitly say slip-only/no official reporter citation.

reasons: The opinion analyzes LPR-derived vehicle-location data under Carpenter, Knotts, CSLI, and geofence comparisons.
The text states the LPR system was more analogous to Knotts beeper signals than CSLI and that the instant LPR technology provided only periodic vehicle-location information.
Lake identity confirms this is a Fifth Circuit court-of-appeals case, supporting the lower-court-development role.
residual_risks: The destination home page itself is not disclosed, so this verifies only the case-to-home fit from the opinion text and content-page taxonomy.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Consider phrasing the role as lower-court ALPR/public-movements development distinguished from CSLI.

reasons: The opening paragraph states that use of an LPR did not constitute a search, no warrant was required, the stop was supported by reasonable suspicion, the Glock and switch were found in plain view, circuit precedent foreclosed the Second Amendment challenge, and the judgment was affirmed.
The LPR section supports the public-road/fixed-camera framing by describing scans when a vehicle passes one of the stationed cameras and emphasizing periodic public-street information.
The stop and plain-view sections separately uphold reasonable suspicion and the district court's finding that Hoggard saw the Glock and switch in plain view.
residual_risks: The no-search statement is strongest when tied to the limited LPR system in the instant case, not all ALPR networks or long-term historical tracking systems.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Add 'on these facts' or 'the limited Gautier LPR system' before the no-search rule.
